title: Hebe, cupbearer of the gods
greek: πότνια Ἥβη (potnia Hēbē), lady Hebe; ἥβη, youth
short: Book IV opens on Olympus, where Hebe ('Youth') pours nectar for the gods as they watch Troy from their golden floor.
body: Hebe's name is the ordinary Greek word for youth or the bloom of youth (ἥβη), and her task of pouring nectar suits it: the gods' drink keeps them ageless. Hesiod makes her the daughter of Zeus and Hera (Theogony 922) and the wife of the deified Heracles (Theogony 950-5); in the Iliad she appears only here and in Book V, where she prepares Hera's chariot and bathes the wounded Ares (5.722, 5.905). Leaf notes that her marriage to Heracles appears in Homer only in a passage of the Odyssey usually regarded as post-Homeric (Od. 11.603). The scene sets up a deliberate contrast: the gods drink and toast one another from golden cups 'as they looked forth upon the city of the Trojans', a city whose fate they are about to decide almost casually. The 'golden floor' (χρυσέῳ ἐν δαπέδῳ) belongs to the general splendour of the gods' house.

title: Alalcomenean Athene (and Argive Hera)
greek: Ἀλαλκομενηῒς Ἀθήνη (Alalkomenēïs Athēnē); Ἥρη Ἀργείη (Hērē Argeiē)
short: Zeus names Menelaus' two divine helpers by their cult titles: Hera of Argos and Athene of Alalcomenae in Boeotia, a title that also suggests 'the Protectress'.
body: Hera is 'Argive' because Argos, with its great sanctuary of Hera, was her chief cult centre (she names it first among her favourite cities at 4.51-2). Athene's title refers to Alalcomenae, a small Boeotian town near Lake Copais where, according to Pausanias, Athene was said to have been reared by the local hero Alalcomeneus; her ancient image there was carried off by Sulla, and a stream nearby was called Triton (Pausanias 9.33.5-7). Leaf adds that the title here becomes descriptive rather than local, 'the Guardian', since it echoes the verb ἀλαλκεῖν, 'to ward off'; the only other Homeric instance is 5.908, where the same two goddesses are paired in the same line. The wordplay matters in this book: within a hundred lines Athene will indeed ward off Pandarus' arrow from Menelaus (4.127-31). Zeus's remark that these two goddesses only 'sit apart and take their pleasure' while Aphrodite actively saves Paris is a deliberate provocation.

title: Zeus and Hera: 'devour Priam raw'
greek: ὠμὸν βεβρώθοις Πρίαμον (ōmon bebrōthois Priamon), you would eat Priam raw
short: Zeus teases Hera, then accuses her of a hatred of Troy so savage that only eating Priam and his sons raw could satisfy it.
body: The divine council begins with Zeus deliberately provoking Hera 'with mocking words' (κερτομίοις ἐπέεσσι): Menelaus has won, so why not make peace and let Troy survive? Hera's fury makes him reply that only by entering Troy and devouring Priam and his sons raw could she 'heal her anger' (χόλον ἐξακέσαιο). The wish to eat an enemy raw is the Iliad's most extreme expression of hatred: Akhilleus says he would like to carve and eat Hector raw (22.346-7), and Hecuba wishes she could bite into Akhilleus' liver (24.212-13). Leaf collects these parallels and compares Xenophon telling his soldiers they must 'eat these men raw' if they can (Anabasis 4.8.14). The scene is a sharp mixture of comedy and horror: an Olympian marital quarrel decides the fate of a city, and the gods' language anticipates the savagery humans will act out later in the poem. Zeus yields 'with soul unwilling', and Troy's doom is sealed by a bargain.

title: 'The equal feast': sacrifice as the gods' due
greek: δαιτὸς ἐΐσης λοιβῆς τε κνίσης τε (daitos eïsēs loibēs te knisēs te); γέρας (geras), prize of honour
short: Zeus loved Troy because its altar never lacked 'the equal feast', libation and the savour of burnt sacrifice: the gods' privilege and share.
body: Zeus explains that of all cities 'beneath sun and starry heaven' sacred Ilios was most honoured in his heart, 'for never at any time was mine altar in lack of the equal feast, the drink-offering, and the savour of burnt-offering, even the worship that is our due' (τὸ γὰρ λάχομεν γέρας ἡμεῖς, 'for that is the privilege we have received as our portion'). δαὶς ἐΐση, 'a fairly divided feast', is the formula for a properly shared banquet in which each receives his due; λοιβή is the poured libation; κνίση the smoke and savour of fat burnt on the altar, which rises to the gods. The relationship is one of reciprocity and honour (τιμή): mortals give the gods their share, and the gods are expected to favour them in return. The tragedy of Troy is that piety does not save it; Zeus repeats the same words at the end of the poem when he insists that Hector, too, never failed in his offerings (24.68-70).

anchor: Argos and Sparta and broad-wayed Mycenae
title: Hera's three cities
greek: Ἄργός τε Σπάρτη τε καὶ εὐρυάγυια Μυκήνη (Argos te Spartē te kai euruaguia Mukēnē)
short: Hera offers Zeus her own favourite cities, Argos, Sparta and Mycenae, to destroy whenever he wishes, in exchange for Troy's ruin.
body: The bargain is chilling: Hera will not defend Argos, Sparta and 'broad-wayed' Mycenae if Zeus ever chooses to sack them, so long as he lets her destroy Troy. The three are the cities of her Achaean favourites: Argos with her great sanctuary, Sparta of Menelaus, Mycenae of Agamemnon. Leaf drew a historical inference: the prominence of the city of Argos here and in Hera's title 'Argive' (4.8) suggests composition after the 'Dorian' upheavals that, in his view, raised Argos at the expense of Mycenae, so that the two could not have flourished side by side as the poem presents them; he thought hearers would apply Hera's words to the fall of Mycenae, the price paid for Troy. Later archaeology has complicated his historical picture, but the passage does let the Greeks' own future ruin into the tragic frame. Hera's argument rests on status: she is Cronos' eldest daughter and Zeus's wife, and 'I also am a god'. The upshot is that Athene is sent to make the Trojans break the truce first, so that the blame falls on them.

anchor: a star to be a portent
title: Athene descends like a shooting star
greek: ἀστέρα ... τέρας (astera ... teras), a star ... a portent
short: Athene darts down from Olympus like a blazing meteor sent by Zeus as a sign, and both armies, amazed, wonder whether war or peace is coming.
body: Zeus's daughter descends 'even in such wise as the son of crooked-counselling Cronos sendeth a star to be a portent (τέρας) for seamen or for a wide host of warriors, a gleaming star, and therefrom the sparks fly thick'. Leaf observes that the comparison implies more than speed, at least a visible flash, since the watching armies marvel; yet Homeric gods do not usually show themselves openly to crowds, and the men do not know what has happened, only that some decisive divine intervention is coming. He compares Athene's descent 'clothed in a cloud like a rainbow' as a portent at 17.547-52, and the Homeric Hymn to Apollo (440-2), where Apollo leaps from a ship 'like a star at midday' with sparks flying, lines that seem to imitate this passage. The soldiers' ambiguous question, war again or friendship, is grimly answered: the goddess has come to wreck the truce.

title: Pandarus, son of Lycaon
greek: Πάνδαρος ἀντίθεος (Pandaros antitheos), godlike Pandarus
short: Athene, disguised as a Trojan, persuades the archer Pandarus to shoot Menelaus and so break the oaths: a fool's bid for glory and gifts.
body: Pandarus leads the Trojans of Zeleia, at the foot of Mount Ida by the river Aesepus; the Catalogue says Apollo himself gave him his bow (2.824-7). Athene comes to him in the likeness of Laodocus, a son of Antenor, and appeals to his vanity and greed: he will win favour with all Trojans and 'glorious gifts' from Paris. The narrator comments that she 'persuaded his heart in his folly' (φρένας ἄφρονι πεῖθεν, 4.104). The episode places responsibility on both levels: a goddess prompts, but a man chooses. Pandarus pays in the next book, when Diomedes' spear shears through his tongue (5.290-6). His name had a long afterlife: medieval and Renaissance versions of the Troy story (Boccaccio's Filostrato, Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde, Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida) turned him into the go-between of the lovers, and from that figure English took the word 'pander'.

title: Apollo Lykēgenēs, 'the wolf-born god'
greek: Ἀπόλλωνι Λυκηγενέϊ κλυτοτόξῳ (Apollōni Lukēgeneï klutotoxōi)
short: Murray renders Lykēgenēs 'wolf-born'; ancient and modern scholars have also explained it as 'born in Lycia' or 'born of light'.
body: The epithet occurs only here and in the repeated line 4.119. Three explanations go back to antiquity. (1) 'Wolf-born': the wolf was sacred to Apollo, who was worshipped widely as Λύκειος (whence the Lyceum at Athens), and Aristotle reports a legend that Leto turned into a she-wolf when she travelled to Delos to give birth (History of Animals 6.35, 580a); Leaf favours this sense and compares the mouse-title Smintheus (1.39) as a trace of animal cult. (2) 'Born in Lycia': Apollo had famous Lycian shrines, and Pandarus' people are in some versions called Lycians (5.105); Leaf allows that the poet may have had this in mind. (3) 'Born of light' (from a supposed λύκη, light), an interpretation known to Macrobius (Saturnalia 1.17.36-41), which Leaf rejects because compounds in -γενής are passive and the sun-god identification is late. LSJ, by contrast, gives 'Lycian-born' (at Patara) as the usual explanation. The question remains open. What matters in context is that Pandarus vows a hecatomb of firstling lambs to his patron archer-god before shooting.

title: Pandarus' horn bow
greek: τόξον ἐΰξοον ἰξάλου αἰγὸς ἀγρίου (toxon euxoon ixalou aigos agriou); ἑκκαιδεκάδωρα (hekkaidekadōra), sixteen palms long
short: Pandarus' bow is made from the horns of a wild ibex he shot himself, worked by a horn-craftsman and tipped with gold: a composite horn bow.
body: The poet pauses on the weapon's history before it is used, a typical Homeric way of giving an object weight. Pandarus killed the animal from ambush as it came out from a rock; its horns grew 'sixteen palms' long (δῶρον, a palm, four fingers' breadth), and a 'worker in horn' (κεραοξόος τέκτων) fitted them together, smoothed them and set a gold tip (κορώνη) on the end for the string. Leaf identifies the animal as the ibex, extinct in mainland Greece but known in Crete, where a bronze plate shows a hunter carrying a bow apparently made of ibex horns; he notes that four-foot horns would be exceptionally long, so the poet may be exaggerating or giving the combined length. The archery sequence that follows is unusually detailed: the bow braced against the ground, comrades shielding the archer, the arrow 'that had never been shot', the string drawn to the breast, the twang. The slow-motion telling makes the treacherous shot momentous.

title: 'Freighted with dark pains' (herma odynaōn)
greek: μελαινέων ἕρμ' ὀδυνάων (melaineōn herm' odunaōn)
short: The arrow is called 'a herma of dark pains', a famous crux; Murray's 'freighted' follows the sense 'ballast, cargo' suggested by Leaf.
body: ἕρμα in Homer means a prop set under a beached ship (1.486), metaphorically a 'prop' or stay of a city (16.549), and, in the plural, earrings (14.182); the senses 'ballast' and 'reef' appear only later (Leaf; LSJ records 'reef' from the archaic poets on). The usual explanation, 'foundation (or source) of dark pains', seemed so odd to Aristarchus that he rejected the line as absurd, yet Apollonius of Rhodes imitated it, which shows it is old. Leaf, admitting that no explanation is fully satisfactory, suggests that the later sense 'ballast' points to 'cargo, freight of woes', and compares Aeschylus, Suppliants 580, where an unborn child is a 'freight' (ἕρμα) of Zeus. Murray's 'freighted with dark pains' follows that interpretation. Either way the phrase loads a single small arrow with all the suffering that will follow from the broken truce.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 4.4.117

title: The iron arrow-head
greek: τόξῳ δὲ σίδηρον (toxōi de sidēron), and the iron to the bow
short: Pandarus draws 'the iron arrow-head' to the bow: the only iron weapon-point in Homer, a sign of the poet's Iron Age world behind a Bronze Age setting.
body: Homeric heroes fight with bronze (χαλκός); the poem's own formulas speak of 'the pitiless bronze' and 'bronze that cleaveth the flesh' (4.511). Iron (σίδηρος) appears as a precious metal, as a prize, and in tools: in this very book a wainwright fells a poplar 'with the gleaming iron' (4.485). Leaf notes that this line gives the only iron weapon-point in Homer, apart from the iron club of Areithous (7.141), and that some critics condemned the line for that reason, a step he calls arbitrary; he takes it as one sign that Book IV belongs to a later stage of epic composition. The detail is a reminder that the poems were shaped by singers living in the Iron Age, who preserved much Bronze Age material but let their own world show through, especially in similes and incidental details.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 4.4.123

title: The narrator addresses Menelaus (apostrophe)
greek: οὐδὲ σέθεν Μενέλαε θεοὶ μάκαρες λελάθοντο (oude sethen Menelae theoi makares lelathonto)
short: At the moment of danger the narrator turns and speaks to Menelaus directly, 'Then, O Menelaus', a rare device in Homer that signals sympathy.
body: Homer's narrator seldom speaks in his own person, but occasionally he addresses a character in the second person (apostrophe). In the Iliad this happens most often with Menelaus (here and at 4.146, and later at 7.104, 13.603, 17.679, 17.702 and 23.600) and with Patroclus in Book XVI as his death approaches; in the Odyssey it is the swineherd Eumaeus. Some have explained it as a metrical convenience, but its distribution suggests more: it falls on characters the poet treats with special warmth, and at moments of danger. Elizabeth Block argued that apostrophe briefly closes the distance between narrator and character, drawing the audience into concern for him. Here it introduces the tender image of Athene sweeping the arrow aside like a mother brushing a fly from her sleeping child, and returns in the ivory simile ('even in such wise, Menelaus, were thy thighs stained with blood').

title: Athene Ageleiē, 'driver of the spoil'
greek: Διὸς θυγάτηρ ἀγελείη (Dios thugatēr ageleiē)
short: Athene's epithet ageleiē is traditionally understood as 'she who drives off the booty', a goddess of raids, from ἄγω (drive) and λεία (plunder).
body: ἀγελείη is used only of Athene. Leaf follows the traditional derivation from ἄγειν, 'to drive', and λεία (ληΐς), 'booty', so that the title presents her as patron of cattle-raids and plunder; he points to her epithet ληΐτις, 'goddess of spoil', at 10.460, where Odysseus dedicates Dolon's spoils to her. The title is pointed here: the warlike goddess of plunder stoops to an act of maternal tenderness, and her protection of Menelaus serves her larger aim, the destruction of Troy. Note also the grammar Leaf points out: 'first of all' (πρώτη) follows the negative 'forgat thee not' as if the poet had said 'remembered thee'.

anchor: as a mother sweepeth a fly
title: Athene turns the arrow: the mother and the fly
greek: ὡς ὅτε μήτηρ παιδὸς ἐέργῃ μυῖαν (hōs hote mētēr paidos eergēi muian); μίτρη (mitrē), taslet
short: Athene brushes the arrow aside as easily as a mother sweeps a fly from her sleeping child, guiding it to where Menelaus' armour is thickest.
body: A domestic simile of great tenderness interrupts the treachery: the goddess deflects the arrow 'just aside from the flesh, even as a mother sweepeth a fly from her child when he lieth in sweet slumber'. The image conveys both the ease of divine power and its protectiveness. She directs the arrow to the point where the golden clasps of the belt (ζωστήρ) meet and the corselet overlaps, so that it must pierce several layers: the belt, the corselet, and the 'taslet' (μίτρη), which LSJ describes as apparently a metal guard worn round the waist, 'a screen for his flesh and a barrier (ἕρκος) against darts', and also the kilt (ζῶμα, 4.187). Murray's archaic 'taslet' (a piece of armour guarding the thighs) renders a word whose exact form is uncertain. Leaf notes that some ancient editors read ἔλυμα, 'wrap, covering', instead of ἔρυμα, 'screen', and thinks the rarer word may be original. The arrow only grazes the skin, but the dark blood flows, leading to the next, startling simile.

title: Ivory stained with scarlet (simile)
greek: ὡς δ' ὅτε τίς τ' ἐλέφαντα γυνὴ φοίνικι μιήνῃ Μῃονὶς ἠὲ Κάειρα (hōs d' hote tis t' elephanta gunē phoinikī miēnēi Mēionis ēe Kaeira)
short: Menelaus' blood on his thighs is compared to scarlet dye on ivory, worked by a Maeonian or Carian woman into a royal cheek-piece for a horse.
body: The wound is described through a craft image from Asia Minor: a woman of Maeonia (Lydia) or Caria stains ivory with crimson (φοῖνιξ, the purple-red dye associated with Phoenicia) to make a cheek-piece for a horse's bridle, which lies in a treasure-chamber, coveted by many horsemen but kept for a king, 'alike an ornament for his horse and to its driver a glory'. The simile turns injury into an object of beauty and value, and the contrast of white skin and red blood is its visual core. The ivory and the luxury trade of Anatolia also hint at the world of the Trojans' allies. Virgil remembered the image in a very different setting, Lavinia's blush: 'as when someone stains Indian ivory with blood-red purple' (Aeneid 12.67-9). The apostrophe 'even in such wise, Menelaus, were thy thighs stained' keeps the narrator's sympathy in view.

anchor: day shall come when sacred Ilios
title: 'The day shall come when sacred Ilios shall be laid low'
greek: ἔσσεται ἦμαρ ὅτ' ἄν ποτ' ὀλώλῃ Ἴλιος ἱρή (essetai ēmar hot' an pot' olōlēi Ilios hirē)
short: Agamemnon is sure that Zeus will punish the broken oath, if late; his prophecy of Troy's fall is the line Scipio quoted as Carthage burned.
body: Agamemnon's speech over his wounded brother states the theology of the oath: an oath sealed with 'the blood of lambs and drink-offerings of unmixed wine and the hand-clasps' is never in vain, for 'even if for the moment the Olympian vouchsafeth not fulfillment, yet late and at length doth he fulfill them', and the guilty pay 'with their own heads and their wives and their children' (4.158-62). Then comes the prophecy: 'the day shall come when sacred Ilios shall be laid low, and Priam, and the people of Priam, with goodly spear of ash.' Hector repeats the same two lines to Andromache in Book VI (6.448-9), as a premonition rather than a threat. Leaf notes that 'with goodly spear of ash' (ἐυμμελίω) is an odd epithet for the aged Priam, who is not shown as a warrior. Polybius, who was present, records that Scipio Aemilianus, watching Carthage burn in 146 BC, wept and recited these lines, thinking that Rome too might one day fall (Polybius 38.22, preserved by Appian, Punica 132). The speech then turns to Agamemnon's fear of shame if Menelaus dies: he imagines a Trojan leaping on his brother's barrow and jeering, a taunt whose opening 'Would that...' (αἴθ') Leaf finds bitterly ironic, and he ends 'let the wide earth gape for me'.

title: 'Thirsty Argos'
greek: πολυδίψιον Ἄργος (poludipsion Argos), very thirsty Argos
short: Agamemnon fears returning in disgrace to 'thirsty Argos'; ancient critics argued over why Argos, which has many wells, should be called thirsty.
body: πολυδίψιος means 'very thirsty, parched' (LSJ). The epithet puzzled ancient readers, since the Argive plain is watered by streams and shallow wells. Strabo rejects the idea of a waterless Argos as a fiction, reviews interpretations of the word (some took it as 'much longed for'), and argues that Homer means the Peloponnese as a whole (Geography 8.6.7). He also cites the legend that the daughters of Danaus discovered the wells of Argos, and quotes the line 'Argos, which was waterless, the daughters of Danaus made well-watered', a verse modern editors assign to Hesiod (Strabo 8.6.8). Leaf adds that the rivers by Argos, the Inachus and Charadrus, are almost dry in summer, and that the plain's reputation for good water rested on irrigation, to which the legends allude. In Agamemnon's mouth it adds to the bleakness of his imagined homecoming: an empty-handed return to a dry land, while Menelaus' bones rot at Troy and Trojans leap on his barrow.

title: Machaon, son of Asclepius, and Cheiron's drugs
greek: Ἀσκληπιοῦ υἱὸν ἀμύμονος ἰητῆρος (Asklēpiou huion amumonos iētēros); Χείρων (Cheirōn)
short: Machaon, son of the 'peerless physician' Asclepius, treats Menelaus: Homer's clearest scene of battlefield medicine.
body: In Homer Asclepius is not yet a god but a mortal 'peerless physician' (ἀμύμων ἰητήρ), whose sons Machaon and Podalirius lead the men of Tricca in Thessaly (2.729-33; Murray's 'Trica' reflects the spelling Τρίκη used here, as Leaf notes). Machaon's treatment follows a clear order: he draws out the arrow (its barbs bend back as it comes), loosens the belt, kilt and taslet, examines the wound, sucks out the blood, and spreads on 'soothing simples' (ἤπια φάρμακα) which the centaur Cheiron had given to his father 'with kindly thought'. Cheiron, called 'most just of the Centaurs' (11.832), also taught medicine to Akhilleus, and in later myth he was the teacher of Asclepius himself (Pindar, Pythian 3.1-7, 45-6). Leaf notes that Homer mentions Cheiron's teaching of medicine to Akhilleus (11.832) and his gift of the ash spear to Peleus (16.143), but no other legends about him; he also rejects Pausanias' view that φῶτα in 4.194 means 'mortal son' as opposed to a divine father. The healer's value is stated later by Idomeneus: 'a leech is worth many other men' (11.514). Later tradition deified Asclepius, whose cult flourished at Epidaurus and Cos.

title: The Review of the troops (Epipolesis)
greek: ἐπιπώλησις (epipōlēsis), going round, inspection; ἐπεπωλεῖτο στίχας ἀνδρῶν (epepōleito stichas andrōn)
short: Agamemnon goes round the army on foot, praising the eager and rebuking the hesitant: the 'Review', a catalogue in action that characterises the leaders.
body: The long section 4.223-421 is one of the episodes named by ancient scholars: the Epipolesis, 'going round' or 'inspection', from the verb ἐπεπωλεῖτο, 'he ranged through' (4.231, 4.250). It opens with a narrator's address to an imagined spectator: 'then wouldst thou not have seen goodly Agamemnon slumbering, nor cowering' (οὐκ ἂν βρίζοντα ἴδοις); Leaf notes the construction, 'you would not have seen', as in 'thou wouldst not have deemed' at 4.429. Agamemnon leaves his chariot with his squire and goes on foot. Two kinds of speech alternate: encouragement to the eager (Idomeneus, the Aiantes, Nestor) and rebuke to those apparently holding back (Menestheus and Odysseus, Diomedes and Sthenelus). Each encounter shows character: Idomeneus loyal, Nestor nostalgic, Odysseus stung and sharp, Diomedes silent and respectful, Sthenelus boastful. Like the Catalogue of Ships and the View from the Wall, the Review introduces the main Achaean heroes before the fighting, and it shows Agamemnon at his most energetic, though his rebukes are not always fair.

title: Iomoroi: an insult of uncertain meaning
greek: Ἀργεῖοι ἰόμωροι ἐλεγχέες (Argeioi iomōroi elencheēs)
short: Agamemnon calls the laggards iomōroi, a word Murray renders 'that rage with the bow'; its meaning was already disputed in antiquity.
body: The insult ἰόμωροι recurs only once in the Iliad (14.479), and both halves of the word are uncertain. Leaf sets out the options: (1) from ἰός, 'arrow', as ἐγχεσίμωρος is formed from ἔγχος, 'spear', so 'devoted to the bow', which Murray follows with 'that rage with the bow'; to call a spearman an archer was to call him a coward who fights from a distance, as Diomedes taunts Paris (11.385-7); (2) from ἰά, 'voice', 'mighty in shouting', and nothing else; (3) a reference to dark hair, which Leaf thinks improbable. Agamemnon pairs it with ἐλεγχέες, which Leaf would correct to ἐλέγχεα, 'things of shame', a neuter that 'adds a sting', and continues with a simile: the men stand dazed like fawns that have run themselves out on a wide plain and stand still with no courage in them. Leaf thought the question 'why have you come to a stand?' and the fawn simile better suited to a sudden halt in pursuit, and suspected they were composed for another context. His sarcastic question, whether they are waiting for the Trojans to reach the ships to see if Zeus will hold his hand over them, anticipates exactly what will happen in the middle books of the poem.

title: Honour at the feast: Idomeneus' full cup
greek: γερούσιον αἴθοπα οἶνον (gerousion aithopa oinon), the flaming wine of the elders; δαιτρόν (daitron), allotted portion
short: Agamemnon flatters Idomeneus with the most visible sign of honour among chieftains: at feasts his cup, like the king's, is always kept full.
body: Homeric honour (τιμή) is concrete: it is shown in seats, portions of meat and wine. At the elders' banquets, where the leading Argives mix 'the flaming wine of the elders' (γερούσιον οἶνον), the others drink an allotted portion (δαιτρόν), but Idomeneus, like Agamemnon himself, has a cup that 'standeth ever full, to drink whensoever thy heart biddeth thee'. The privilege brings an obligation to fight in the front line: Sarpedon makes the same argument at length in 12.310-21, where seats of honour, meat and full cups oblige the Lycian kings to lead the battle. Agamemnon later uses the reverse argument against Menestheus and Odysseus, who are 'first to hear my bidding to the feast' but slow to fight (4.343-8). Leaf compares Diomedes' honours of 'meat and fuller cups' (8.161-2) and the biblical 'Benjamin's mess', five times as large as his brothers' (Genesis 43:34). Idomeneus, the Cretan king, answers with a pledge of loyalty and turns the talk back to the broken oaths.

title: The goatherd and the storm cloud; the Aiantes
greek: νέφος αἰπόλος ἀνήρ (nephos aipolos anēr); Αἴαντε (Aiante), the two Aiases
short: The dark mass of troops following the two Aiantes is compared to a storm cloud a goatherd sees coming over the sea, blacker than pitch.
body: The simile is told from the goatherd's viewpoint: from a lookout he sees a cloud driven over the sea by the West Wind, which seems to him, far off, 'blacker than pitch' and brings a great squall (Leaf defends 'blacker than pitch' as no mere hyperbole, since a thunder-cloud is dead in hue while pitch has bright reflections); he shudders and drives his flock into a cave. The listener sees the 'dark battalions, bristling with shields and spears' as the enemy would, as a threat rolling in. As Leaf notes, the simile expands the metaphor of 4.274, 'a cloud of footmen' (νέφος πεζῶν). The leaders are 'the Aiantes', a dual form. Usually it means the two Aiases, the great Aias son of Telamon and the lesser Aias son of Oileus, who, Leaf observes, are always represented as fighting side by side (13.701ff.); but D. L. Page argued that the dual was originally 'elliptic', naming one hero and implying his partner, and meant 'Aias and his brother' Teucer; Gregory Nagy discusses the debate and an ancient scholium (on 13.197) already comments on the poet's continual use of the dual. Agamemnon tells them that if all had their spirit, Priam's city would soon bow her head.

title: Nestor's battle-order and memories
greek: ὧδε καὶ οἱ πρότεροι πόλεας καὶ τείχε' ἐπόρθεον (hōde kai hoi proteroi poleas kai teiche' eporthеon)
short: Nestor marshals the Pylians, chariots in front, good infantry behind, cowards in the middle, and appeals to the methods of the men of old.
body: Nestor, 'the clear-voiced orator of the Pylians', arranges his men: the charioteers with their horses in front, the many brave foot-soldiers behind as 'a bulwark of battle' (ἕρκος πολέμοιο), and the cowards in the middle so that they must fight whether they will or not. He orders the drivers to keep their line and to thrust with the spear when they meet an enemy chariot. This is one of the few places in Homer where chariots seem to be used as a massed fighting arm rather than as transport to and from the front, and scholars have debated whether Nestor's tactics preserve a memory of Bronze Age chariot warfare or are the poet's own invention. Leaf observes that Homeric heroes normally use chariots only to move about and dismount to fight (with exceptions such as 5.13); he found the sudden shift into direct speech strange, thought lines 308-9 suit siege warfare rather than charioteers, saw Attic forms in 308, and judged the passage one of several 'tactical' insertions put into Nestor's mouth, perhaps under Athenian influence. Nestor characteristically appeals to the past ('thus also did men of olden time lay waste cities and walls') and, answering Agamemnon, recalls his youthful killing of Ereuthalion, a story he tells in full at 7.136-56.

title: 'What word hath escaped the barrier of thy teeth?'
greek: ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων (poion se epos phugen herkos odontōn)
short: Odysseus, wrongly accused of hanging back, answers Agamemnon with a formula of indignant surprise and names himself 'the father of Telemachus'.
body: ἕρκος ὀδόντων, 'the fence of the teeth', is a traditional image of the mouth as an enclosure through which words should not escape carelessly; the line is a formula of rebuke used several times in the Odyssey (e.g. Od. 1.64, Zeus to Athene). Agamemnon has accused Menestheus and Odysseus of cowering, and taunted them with their privileges at the feast. Odysseus' reply is sharp: Agamemnon will see 'the father of Telemachus' mingling with the foremost fighters. His self-description through his son occurs only here and at 2.260 in the Iliad, and it links the Iliad's Odysseus to the hero of the other poem; Leaf reports that Aristarchus noticed this 'foreshadowing of the Odyssey' and took it as a sign that both poems were by the same author. Agamemnon at once retracts with a smile, 'when he knew that he was wroth': a quick reconciliation that contrasts with his quarrel with Akhilleus in Book I.

title: Tydeus at Thebes: Agamemnon's paradigm
greek: Τυδεύς (Tudeus); Πολυνείκης (Poluneikēs); Καδμεῖοι (Kadmeioi), Thebans
short: To shame Diomedes, Agamemnon tells how his father Tydeus, envoy to Thebes before the war of the Seven, defeated the Thebans single-handed.
body: The story belongs to the Theban saga, the war of the Seven against Thebes that preceded the Trojan War by a generation. Tydeus, an Aetolian exile, came with Polyneices to Mycenae to recruit allies for Polyneices' attack on his brother Eteocles; the Mycenaeans were willing, but Zeus turned them away with bad omens. Sent ahead as envoy, Tydeus found the Thebans feasting in Eteocles' house, challenged them to contests and won them all, 'such a helper was Athene to him'. On his way back he killed all fifty men set in ambush except Maeon, whom he spared in obedience to the gods. Apollodorus tells the same story (Library 3.6.5). Agamemnon uses it as a paradigm, a story from the past meant to shape present conduct, and ends with a calculated insult: Diomedes is worse than his father in battle, though better in the assembly. Athene repeats the story and the comparison in Book V (5.800-13); Leaf thought it was adapted from epic poems on the Theban war. The theme of fathers and sons runs through Diomedes' whole role in the poem.

title: Diomedes' silence: aidōs
greek: αἰδεσθεὶς βασιλῆος ἐνιπὴν αἰδοίοιο (aidestheis basilēos enipēn aidoioio)
short: Diomedes answers Agamemnon's unfair rebuke with silence, 'out of respect' (aidōs) for the king; he will reply only much later, in Book IX.
body: αἰδώς is the sense of respect and shame that restrains a person before those whose opinion matters; the line plays on it twice: 'respecting (αἰδεσθείς) the rebuke of the respected (αἰδοίοιο) king'. Unlike Odysseus and Sthenelus, Diomedes swallows the insult, explaining to Sthenelus that the commander must urge the army on, since glory or grief will fall on him. His restraint makes him the model of the young warrior who accepts hierarchy, the opposite of Akhilleus in Book I. But he does not forget: in Book IX, when Agamemnon proposes flight, Diomedes reminds him, 'You first reviled my valour among the Danaans' (9.32-6). Douglas Cairns' study of aidos uses Homeric scenes like this to show how the emotion governs relations of status. The section ends as Diomedes leaps from his chariot, the bronze ringing terribly on his chest, a preface to his great exploits in Book V.

title: Sthenelus and the Epigoni
greek: ἡμεῖς τοι πατέρων μέγ' ἀμείνονες εὐχόμεθ' εἶναι (hēmeis toi paterōn meg' ameinones eukhometh' einai)
short: Sthenelus retorts that the sons are better than their fathers: they, the Epigoni, took seven-gated Thebe where the Seven had failed.
body: Sthenelus is the son of Capaneus, one of the Seven who died at Thebes, and he fought with Diomedes among the Epigoni ('Afterborn'), the sons of the Seven who returned a generation later and sacked the city (Apollodorus 3.7.2-4). He answers for his silent friend: 'we declare ourselves to be better men by far than our fathers', for with a smaller army they took the city, trusting in the portents of the gods and the help of Zeus, while their fathers 'perished through their own blind folly' (ἀτασθαλίῃσιν). Leaf notes that this is Homer's only mention of the war of the Epigoni, and illustrates the fathers' 'blind folly' from Aeschylus' Capaneus, who boasts he will sack Thebes whether the god wills it or not (Seven against Thebes 427ff.). Sthenelus' boast reverses the usual Homeric assumption, voiced by Nestor (1.260-72), that earlier generations were stronger. Hesiod places the heroes who fought at seven-gated Thebe and at Troy together in the Age of Heroes (Works and Days 161-5). Diomedes silences him with 'Good friend' (τέττα), a rare, affectionate address.

title: The silent Danaans and the bleating Trojans
greek: ἀλλὰ γλῶσσα μέμικτο, πολύκλητοι δ' ἔσαν ἄνδρες (alla glōssa memikto, poluklētoi d' esan andres)
short: Two contrasting similes: the Danaans advance like waves, rank after rank, in silence; the Trojans bleat like ewes, for their allies speak many languages.
body: As battle is finally joined, Homer returns to the contrast with which Book III began (Leaf points to 3.1-9). The Danaan battalions move 'rank after rank, without cease', like waves driven by the West Wind that rise out at sea, break thundering on the shore and spit out brine round the headlands; each captain gives his orders, and the rest march in silence 'through fear of their commanders'. The Trojans, by contrast, are like countless ewes in a rich man's yard, bleating ceaselessly as they hear their lambs, 'for they had not all like speech or one language, but their tongues were mingled, and they were a folk summoned from many lands' (πολύκλητοι, 'called together from many parts', Leaf). Iris had made the same point in Book II (2.803-4), advising Hector to have each leader command his own people. The contrast is not only of discipline: it presents the Achaeans as one people and the Trojan side as a multilingual coalition of Anatolian allies.

title: Eris (Strife), Terror and Rout
greek: Δεῖμός τ' ἠδὲ Φόβος καὶ Ἔρις ἄμοτον μεμαυῖα (Deimos t' ēde Phobos kai Eris amoton memauia)
short: Ares and Athene drive on the armies, with Terror, Rout and Eris (Strife), who starts small but soon plants her head in heaven while walking on earth.
body: Abstract powers of war take the field as personified figures. Δεῖμος (Terror) and Φόβος (Rout, panic flight) are elsewhere sons of Ares (13.299, 15.119; Hesiod, Theogony 934); Ἔρις, Strife, 'sister and comrade of man-slaying Ares', is pictured growing (Leaf stresses that these half-personified spirits of battle stir up both armies alike and take no side): 'at the first she rears her crest but little, yet thereafter planteth her head in heaven, while her feet tread on earth'. The image catches how a quarrel escalates. Virgil borrowed it for Fama (Rumour), who is 'small at first through fear, soon lifts herself into the air, walks on the ground and hides her head among the clouds' (Aeneid 4.176-7). Macrobius, comparing the two passages, judged Homer's version apt and Virgil's inapt: strife remains strife however large it grows, but a rumour so great that everyone knows it is no longer rumour (Saturnalia 5.13.31-2). Leaf, who notes the imitation, regarded such personifications as unlike the older epic manner. Eris returns at the start of Book XI, sent by Zeus to the Achaean ships (11.3-14).

title: The armies meet like mountain torrents
greek: χείμαρροι ποταμοί ... ἐς μισγάγκειαν (cheimarroi potamoi ... es misgankeian)
short: The armies clash like two winter torrents meeting in a ravine, whose roar a shepherd hears far off in the mountains.
body: The first general engagement of the poem is described in a sequence of grand, formulaic lines: shields, spears and the fury of bronze-clad men clash together, bossed shields close, the groaning of the dying mingles with the boasting of the killers, 'and the earth flowed with blood'. Then comes the simile: winter torrents running down from great springs join their mighty floods at a μισγάγκεια, a word found only here, which Leaf renders 'watersmeet', the place where two valleys (ἄγκεα) join their streams, and pour into a deep gorge, while far off a shepherd hears the thunder. The key idea is mixing (μισγομένων, 'as they mingled', 4.456): two masses becoming one confused roar. As often, the simile places a distant, peaceful observer at the edge of violence, like the goatherd of 4.275-9.

title: The first kill: Antilochus and Echepolus
greek: τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψεν (ton de skotos osse kalupsen), darkness covered his eyes
short: The poem's first killing in battle: Antilochus, Nestor's son, spears Echepolus through the forehead; a fight over the corpse follows at once.
body: After three and a half books, the fighting begins with a named kill. Antilochus, the young son of Nestor, who appears here for the first time (Leaf), strikes Echepolus on the ridge of his helmet and drives the spear into his forehead: 'darkness enfolded his eyes, and he crashed as doth a wall' (the Greek says 'like a tower', πύργος). The death-formula 'darkness enfolded his eyes' (σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψεν) appears here for the first time. At once comes a typical sequel: Elephenor, leader of the Abantes from Euboea, tries to drag the body away to strip its armour, exposes his side as he stoops, and is killed by Agenor; a struggle over the corpse follows, the men leaping on each other 'even as wolves'. The pattern of kill, attempt to strip, counter-kill recurs throughout the battle books. Stripping an enemy's armour was a mark of victory, which makes the rescue of bodies so fiercely contested.

title: Simoeisius and the poplar
greek: Σιμοείσιος (Simoeisios), 'of the Simois'; θρέπτρα (threptra), return for nurture; αἴγειρος (aigeiros), poplar
short: Aias kills the young Simoeisius, named after the river by which he was born; a brief 'obituary' and a poplar simile make him the first victim we mourn.
body: Simoeisius' mother bore him on the banks of the Simois, Troy's river, as she came down from Ida with her parents to see their flocks, 'for this cause they called him Simoeisius'. He never repaid his parents for his rearing (θρέπτρα), and his life was short. Leaf compares other Trojans named after rivers, Satnius (14.443) and Scamandrius, Hector's son Astyanax (6.402); θρέπτρα, the 'recompense for rearing', is what a grown child owes his parents. Jasper Griffin drew attention to such brief biographies of minor warriors, given at the moment of death, which create pathos by recalling the peaceful world the victim leaves. The simile then shows him falling like a smooth poplar grown in a water-meadow, cut down by a wainwright with gleaming iron to bend into the rim of a chariot wheel (a soft wood, Leaf notes, but valued for its flexibility), left drying by a river: the river-born youth dies by a river image, and the tree is turned into an instrument of war. The killing provokes a chain of revenge, Antiphus, Leucus, Odysseus, Democoon, typical of the battle narrative.

title: Apollo from Pergamus: 'Achilles fighteth not'
greek: Περγάμου ἐκκατιδών (Pergamou ekkatidōn); χόλον θυμαλγέα πέσσει (cholon thumalgea pessei)
short: Apollo, watching from Troy's citadel Pergamus, rallies the Trojans: the Achaeans are not made of stone, and Akhilleus is 'nursing his bitter wrath' by the ships.
body: Pergamus (Πέργαμος) is the citadel of Troy, where Apollo has his temple (5.446); in Latin poetry 'Pergama' becomes a name for Troy itself. From there Apollo shouts encouragement: the Achaeans' flesh is not stone or iron to resist bronze, and Akhilleus, son of fair-haired Thetis, is not fighting but 'nurseth his bitter wrath' amid the ships. The Greek verb πέσσει means 'cooks, digests', so the anger is pictured as something kept simmering or digested slowly (LSJ s.v. πέσσω); χόλος is literally 'bile'. In Book I Calchas uses the compound καταπέψῃ of a king who 'swallows down' (literally 'digests') his anger for a day but keeps his grudge (1.81-2). Leaf notes that Pergamus is connected with πύργος, 'tower', German Burg. It is the first mention of Akhilleus since Book II and reminds the audience that the whole battle is fought in the shadow of his wrath, the subject announced in the poem's first line.

title: Tritogeneia (Athene)
greek: Τριτογένεια (Tritogeneia)
short: Athene's title Tritogeneia was explained in antiquity as 'born by the Triton' (a river or lake) or 'born from the head'; its meaning is uncertain.
body: The title appears three times in the Iliad (4.515, 8.39, 22.183) and in Hesiod, who uses it of Athene born from Zeus's head (Theogony 924). Ancient explanations vary. Many linked it to a river or lake Triton: the Libyan Lake Tritonis, whose nymph Herodotus makes the mother, with Poseidon, of a Libyan Athene (4.180), or the Boeotian stream Triton at Alalcomenae, where, Pausanias says, she was reared (9.33.7). LSJ lists still other ancient guesses: born on the third day of the month, or the third child after Apollo and Artemis. Leaf mentions the suggestion that a stem τριτο- meant 'water' (as perhaps in Triton and Amphitrite), and rejects as unconfirmed the derivation, reported by Eustathius, from an alleged word τριτώ, 'head', which would make her 'born from the head'. He concludes that the original meaning 'is not now to be discovered'. The local Boeotian connection would link it with her other title in this book, 'Alalcomenean' (4.8). The appearance of Athene urging on the Achaeans here balances Apollo rallying the Trojans: the two gods set the sides against each other.

title: The imagined observer: closing the book
greek: ἄγοι δέ ἑ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη χειρὸς ἑλοῦσ' (agoi de he Pallas Athēnē cheiros helous')
short: After the deaths of Diores and Peiros, the book ends by imagining an unwounded spectator led through the battle by Athene: none could make light of that fighting.
body: The last fights of the book pair two leaders: Diores of the Epeians, crushed by a stone thrown by the Thracian Peiros and disembowelled by his spear, and Peiros himself, killed by Thoas of Aetolia, who cannot strip the armour because Peiros' Thracian comrades, 'that wear the hair long at the top' (ἀκρόκομοι, with a top-knot), drive him back. The two lie 'stretched in the dust each by the other', a grim image of equality in death. Homer then closes the book with a hypothetical observer: a man untouched by missile or thrust, led by the hand of Pallas Athene and shielded by her from the weapons, could no longer find fault with the fighting (ἔργον ὀνόσαιτο), for many Trojans and Achaeans lay face down in the dust side by side. Leaf explains οὐκέτι as 'it had now come to this, that none could make light of it', and compares the 'long hair behind' of the Abantes (2.542) for the Thracians' hairstyle. The device frames the battle as a spectacle for an ideal witness, much as the poem's audience watches it in safety.
